why.correct: A rising concentration of a product means the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction at that moment. The rates become equal only when the curve levels off.
options: Right: [NO₂] is still rising at 20 s, so NO₂ forms faster than it turns back into N₂O₄.
Equal rates would make the curve flat. At 20 s the curve is still climbing, so the rates are not yet equal.
This treats the reaction as one-way. As soon as some NO₂ exists, NO₂ molecules collide and re-form N₂O₄, so the reverse reaction runs from the start.
If the reverse rate were larger, [NO₂] would be falling. It is rising.

why.correct: At equilibrium [NO₂] = 0.0400 M. The 2 : 1 ratio means N₂O₄ fell by 0.0400 M ÷ 2 = 0.0200 M. So [N₂O₄] = 0.0500 M − 0.0200 M = 0.0300 M.
A flat concentration curve means the rate at which NO₂ forms equals the rate at which it is used up. Both reactions keep running.
options: Right: both reactions continue, and equal rates cancel in their effect on concentration. This is a dynamic equilibrium.
From the 2 : 1 ratio, 0.0300 M N₂O₄ is still present. It has not run out; it reacts as fast as it is re-formed.
The temperature is held constant and gas molecules keep colliding. Equilibrium is not a halt in motion.
At equilibrium [N₂O₄] = 0.0300 M and [NO₂] = 0.0400 M. Equilibrium means constant concentrations, not equal ones.

why.correct: Equilibrium can be reached from either direction. 0.100 M NO₂ contains exactly the atoms of 0.0500 M N₂O₄, so at the same temperature the system ends at the same mixture: 0.0400 M NO₂ and 0.0300 M N₂O₄.
options: Right: 0.100 M NO₂ holds the same atoms as 0.0500 M N₂O₄. Same atoms, same volume and same temperature give the same equilibrium mixture, whichever side you start from.
This assumes nothing happens when you start from the product side. NO₂ molecules combine to form N₂O₄ until the rates are equal.
This mirrors the first trial (0.100 − 0.0400) instead of reaching the same mixture. Starting from products, NO₂ falls to the same 0.0400 M.
This halves 0.0400 M as if the 2 : 1 ratio applied to the final concentration. The final mixture is the same as in the first trial.

why.correct: At equilibrium every concentration is constant, so a concentration-time graph becomes a horizontal line.
options: Right: a slope of zero means the concentration is constant, which happens when the forward and reverse rates are equal.
Halfway is just a point on the way up; the concentration is still changing there.
The steepest part is where the forward reaction most outpaces the reverse reaction, the opposite of equilibrium.
No such rule exists. [NO₂] levels off at 0.0400 M, below the starting 0.0500 M of N₂O₄.

why.correct: Equilibrium shows up as a composition that no longer changes with time. The first two snapshots with the same counts are t₂ and t₃.
options: Right: the counts at t₂ and t₃ are the same (3, 3, 6), so the composition has stopped changing by t₂.
The counts change between t₁ and t₂ (XY goes from 4 to 6), so the system was still reacting overall at t₁.
The system is at equilibrium at t₃, but its composition was already the same at t₂.
At t = 0 there is no XY at all, so the reverse reaction cannot yet run and the composition is about to change.

why.correct: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and not zero. The diagrams look the same because the two reactions cancel each other's effect on the counts.
options: Right: equilibrium is dynamic. Individual XY molecules form and fall apart, but as many form as break apart in any stretch of time.
This is the static view of equilibrium. The forward and reverse reactions both continue; they just balance.
If XY only formed, its count would keep rising past 6. The count stays at 6, so XY also breaks apart.
Neither runs out: 3 of each remain at t₂ and t₃. A reversible reaction stops changing well before a reactant is used up.

why.correct: Counts change in the ratio of the coefficients: X₂ goes from 6 to 3 (−3) and XY from 0 to 6 (+6), so 2 XY per X₂.
options: Right: X₂ falls by 3 while XY rises by 6, matching the coefficients 1 and 2 in the equation.
This ignores the coefficient 2 in front of XY. Each X₂ supplies two X atoms, so it ends up in two XY molecules.
Three is how many X₂ molecules reacted, not how many XY form per X₂.
Six is the total number of XY formed. The question asks per X₂ molecule.

why.correct: Equilibrium means the amounts are constant over time, not that they are equal. Here the composition is the same at t₂ and t₃.
options: Right: the test for equilibrium is constant composition. The amounts can be very different from each other.
There are 3 X₂ + 3 Y₂ = 6 reactant molecules and 6 XY, but equality is not the test anyway. Constant counts are.
Nothing about equilibrium fixes it at the halfway point. Where it settles depends on the reaction and the temperature.
Three X₂ molecules remain. A system at equilibrium still holds reactants.

why.correct: Labeled atoms trace individual molecules. Finding the label in HI proves I₂ keeps reacting at equilibrium; HI must also keep breaking down at the same rate, since the concentrations do not change.
options: Right: the labeled I₂ could reach HI only by reacting. Constant concentrations with ongoing reaction is exactly a dynamic equilibrium.
The concentrations were constant before and after the swap. The label simply reveals reactions that were already happening.
The concentrations stay constant, so the rates stay equal. The isotope behaves chemically like ordinary iodine.
Mixing moves molecules around, but it cannot put an iodine atom inside an HI molecule. Bonds had to break and form.

why.correct: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium only in a closed system, where products stay available to react back. An open dish lets CO₂ escape.
options: Right: equilibrium needs a closed system. With the gas leaving, CO₂ can hardly ever collide with CaO to re-form CaCO₃.
Solids can react in both directions; in a sealed container this same reaction does reach equilibrium.
Speed is not the issue: the heated solid does decompose. The problem is that a product leaves the system.
If the reverse reaction were faster, CaCO₃ would form, but the open dish loses CO₂ and the solid keeps decomposing.

why.correct: As reactant is used up, the forward rate falls; as product builds up, the reverse rate rises. When the two meet, the concentrations stop changing.

variables.name: Rate of the forward reaction
variables.why: The forward rate depends on [N₂O₄], which falls as N₂O₄ is used up.

variables.name: Rate of the reverse reaction
variables.why: The reverse rate depends on [NO₂], which rises from zero as NO₂ forms, so NO₂ molecules collide more often.

variables.name: [NO<sub>2</sub>]
variables.why: The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction, so NO₂ builds up.

variables.name: Total mass of gas in the flask
variables.why: The flask is sealed, so no atoms enter or leave; mass is conserved.

why.correct: A reversible reaction starts with the forward rate largest and the reverse rate zero. The rates move toward each other until they are equal: that is chemical equilibrium.
N₂O₄ fell by 0.0800 M − 0.0520 M = 0.0280 M. The coefficients are 1 : 2, so [NO₂] = 2 × 0.0280 M = 0.0560 M.
At chemical equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations are constant. They are usually not equal.
options: Right: equal forward and reverse rates keep every amount steady.
This is the most common misconception. Equilibrium amounts can be very different; they are constant, not equal.
Both reactions continue at equal rates. That is why chemists call it dynamic.
A reaction that goes to completion uses up a reactant. At equilibrium, reactants and products are all present.

why.correct: A reaction rate depends on how often reacting particles collide. As [NO₂] grows, NO₂-NO₂ collisions become more frequent, so the reverse rate rises.
options: Right: the reverse reaction needs two NO₂ molecules to collide. More NO₂ per liter means more such collisions each second.
Molecular speed depends on temperature, which is constant here. The change is in how many NO₂ molecules there are.
Molecules do not push others into reacting. The reverse rate depends on how often NO₂ molecules meet each other.
The reverse reaction does not need energy from the forward reaction to run; it speeds up because its reactant, NO₂, becomes more concentrated.

why.correct: Any measured property that depends on composition, such as color or (when gas moles change) pressure, becomes constant at equilibrium.
options: Right: color tracks the concentration of a colored gas, so a steady color means a steady concentration.
Right: when the number of gas molecules can change, a constant pressure means a constant composition.
Equal amounts are not the test for equilibrium. Constant amounts are.
Steady bubbling means a gas is being produced and leaving, so the composition is still changing.

why.correct: The ⇌ symbol shows a reversible reaction: products can react to re-form the reactants.
options: Right: the symbol marks a reversible reaction.
The symbol says nothing about speed.
The symbol says the reaction is reversible, not how much of each species is present.
Energy changes are shown with ΔH, not with the arrow.

why.correct: Compare the two rates. When the reverse rate is larger, the net reaction runs in reverse: products turn into reactants faster than reactants turn into products.
options: Right: the reverse rate (4.8) is greater than the forward rate (3.0), so isobutane is used faster than it forms.
The way an equation is written does not set the direction. The faster of the two reactions does.
Both reactions happen at every moment once both substances are present. Equilibrium needs the two rates to be equal; 3.0 and 4.8 are not.
More isobutane makes the reverse reaction faster, not the forward one, so the net change is toward butane.

why.correct: A species builds up whenever the reaction that makes it is faster than the reaction that uses it. Here isobutane → butane outpaces butane → isobutane until 150 s.
options: Right: the reverse rate exceeds the forward rate over this whole stretch, so butane accumulates.
The forward reaction does use butane, but the reverse reaction makes it faster still. The net change is an increase.
The total C₄H₁₀ is constant, but the split between the two shapes changes until the rates are equal.
The rising forward rate is a result of rising [butane], not its cause. Butane rises because the reverse reaction is faster.

why.correct: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates are equal. The first row in which they match is 150 s.
options: Right: at 150 s both rates are 4.3 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, and they stay equal at 200 s.
At 80 s the rates are close but not equal (4.2 and 4.3), so there is still a small net reverse reaction.
The system is at equilibrium at 200 s, but the rates were already equal at 150 s.
At 0 s the rates are 3.0 and 4.8, the farthest apart they ever are.

why.correct: A rate depends on the concentration of the species that reacts. The forward reaction uses butane, so as [butane] goes up, so does the forward rate; for the same reason the reverse rate falls as [isobutane] goes down.
options: Right: the forward rate depends on [butane], and [butane] rises as the net reverse reaction runs.
The forward reaction is butane changing shape on the catalyst; isobutane does not drive it. Its rate depends on how much butane there is.
The temperature is constant, so the average speed of the molecules does not change.
A catalyst is not used up, and it speeds the forward and reverse reactions alike.

why.correct: Butane is made by the reverse reaction and used by the forward reaction: net rate = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ M/s − 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
Adding a reactant changes the forward rate first. With the forward rate now larger, the net reaction goes forward until the rates are equal again.
options: Right: more H₂ means more H₂-I₂ collisions each second, so the forward rate jumps while the reverse rate, set by [HI], has not yet changed.
The reverse reaction uses HI, and [HI] did not change at the moment of injection. It is the forward reaction that speeds up.
Only the forward reaction uses H₂. Adding H₂ speeds up that reaction alone, so the rates become unequal.
Rates depend on concentrations as well as temperature. Raising [H₂] raises the rate of the reaction that uses H₂.

why.correct: The direction of a net reaction shows up in which concentrations rise and which fall. After 100 s, HI (product) rises and I₂ (reactant) falls.
options: Right: a product building up while a reactant is used is what a net forward reaction looks like.
The jump is the injection itself, not a reaction. The evidence of reaction is what happens to the concentrations afterward.
That shows H₂ was added, but it does not show a direction; H₂ is higher because only part of the added H₂ reacts.
Flat curves before 100 s show the first equilibrium. They say nothing about what happens after the injection.

why.correct: I₂ fell by 0.0200 M − 0.0103 M = 0.0097 M. Each I₂ that reacts makes 2 HI, so HI rose by 2 × 0.0097 M = 0.0194 M. [HI] = 0.140 M + 0.0194 M = 0.159 M.
At both times forward = reverse. The reverse rate depends on [HI], which is higher at 200 s, so both rates are higher at the new equilibrium.
options: Right: at 200 s [HI] is higher than at 50 s, so the reverse rate is higher; at equilibrium the forward rate equals it.
Both times are at equilibrium, but equilibrium only means forward = reverse. The rates themselves can settle at new values.
At 200 s the system is back at equilibrium, so the two rates are equal again, and [HI] is higher, so the reverse rate has gone up.
Some of the added H₂ reacted, but [H₂] at 200 s is still well above 0.0200 M, and the reverse rate, set by the larger [HI], is higher too.

why.correct: When the forward rate is greater, the net reaction goes forward: reactants decrease and products increase.
options: Right: the forward reaction, which makes SO₃, is faster than the reverse reaction, which uses it.
That would need the reverse reaction to be faster. Here the forward rate is the larger one.
Constant concentrations need equal rates. 5.0 × 10⁻³ and 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s are not equal.
O₂ is used by the faster forward reaction, so it is decreasing.

why.correct: Net change in N₂O₄: 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ − 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, used up. Two NO₂ form per N₂O₄: 2 × 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ M/s.
Removing a product slows the reverse reaction first. The forward reaction is then faster, so the net reaction goes forward until the rates are equal again.

variables.name: Forward rate, at the moment HI is removed
variables.why: The forward rate depends on [H₂] and [I₂], which have not changed at that moment.

variables.name: Reverse rate, at the moment HI is removed
variables.why: Fewer HI molecules per liter means fewer HI-HI collisions each second.

variables.name: [HI] over the next minute
variables.why: With forward faster than reverse, the net reaction goes forward and makes HI back.

variables.name: [H<sub>2</sub>] over the next minute
variables.why: The net forward reaction uses H₂.

why.correct: Adding A changes the forward rate first. The net forward reaction then lowers [A] and raises [B], which pulls the two rates back together at a new equilibrium.
The reverse rate wins when either its reactant (N₂O₄) is added or the forward reaction's reactant (NO₂) is taken away.
options: Right: the reverse reaction uses N₂O₄, so it speeds up first.
Right: the forward reaction uses NO₂, so it slows first, leaving the reverse reaction faster.
More NO₂ speeds up the forward reaction, not the reverse.
Less N₂O₄ slows the reverse reaction, so the forward reaction becomes faster.

why.correct: At equilibrium forward = reverse. A catalyst speeds both reactions by the same factor, so they stay equal and the composition does not change. It only helps a system reach equilibrium sooner.
options: Right: a catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions alike, so the rates stay equal.
A catalyst offers a new pathway for the reaction in both directions. The reverse reaction runs over the same lowered barrier.
The lowered barrier helps both directions equally; neither reaction gains on the other.
A catalyst speeds reactions and is regenerated. It does not remove reactants from the mixture.

why.correct: A product concentration falls only when the reverse reaction outpaces the forward reaction, so the net reaction runs in reverse.
options: Right: CO₂ is made by the forward reaction and used by the reverse one. Falling CO₂ means the reverse reaction is faster.
A faster forward reaction would make CO₂ faster than it is used, so [CO₂] would rise.
The forward reaction runs as long as CO and H₂O are present. It just runs more slowly than the reverse.
H₂ is a product like CO₂, so the net reverse reaction uses it up too: [H₂] is falling.

why.correct: Removing a product as it forms keeps the reverse rate low, so the net reaction keeps going forward. Chemists use this to push reactions toward products.
options: Right: with B constantly removed, the reverse reaction has almost no B to work with, so it cannot catch up.
Equilibrium needs the reverse rate to rise to meet the forward rate. Removing B keeps the reverse rate low.
Equilibrium is set by equal rates, not equal concentrations, and here the rates cannot become equal.
The forward reaction keeps going while A remains. Removing B lets it run until A is nearly used up.

why.correct: Compare Q with K. If Q > K, the mixture has too many products relative to reactants, so the net reaction goes in reverse, lowering Q until Q = K.
options: Right: Q = 400 > K = 280. To lower Q, products must turn back into reactants until Q = K.
This flips the rule. Q > K means the ratio of products to reactants is already too high, so the net reaction runs in reverse.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K, not from comparing amounts in the flask.
Being on the same side of 1 means nothing. The flask is at equilibrium only when Q equals K.

why.correct: A mixture is at equilibrium when Q = K. Only flask 3 has Q ≈ 280.
options: Right: Q = (0.118)² / ((0.0500)² × 0.0200) = 278, equal to K = 280 within the precision of the data.
Q = 80.0 for flask 1, well below K, so it will react forward.
Q = 400 for flask 2, above K, so it will react in reverse.
Flask 4 has no SO₃, so Q = 0. It can only react forward.

why.correct: A mixture with reactants and no products has Q = 0, which is smaller than any K, so it reacts forward.
options: Right: with no product, Q = 0 < K, so the net reaction must go forward.
The forward reaction needs SO₂ and O₂, which are present. Only the reverse reaction lacks a reactant.
Q < K means net forward, which uses SO₂. It cannot form SO₂.
Q can be calculated: zero on top gives Q = 0. Only a zero on the bottom would be a problem.

why.correct: The ratio, not a single concentration, decides direction. Flask 1 has Q = 80.0 < K = 280, so more SO₃ forms until Q = K.
options: Right: the comparison that matters is Q with K, and Q is below K.
The amount of product alone does not decide direction. What matters is the whole ratio Q compared with K.
Q = 80.0 is not 280, so flask 1 is not at equilibrium.
Q is compared with K, not with 1. Here Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward.

why.correct: K<sub>p</sub> has the same form as K<sub>c</sub>, with partial pressures in place of concentrations: products over reactants, each to the power of its coefficient.
options: Right: partial pressures of products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
This is K<sub>c</sub>. Square brackets mean molar concentrations; K<sub>p</sub> uses partial pressures.
Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers.
This is upside down: products go on top.

why.correct: Q<sub>p</sub> < K<sub>p</sub> means too little product for equilibrium, so the net reaction goes forward and P<sub>NH₃</sub> rises until Q<sub>p</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>.
options: Right: 8.33 × 10⁻⁶ < 1.5 × 10⁻⁵, so the net reaction goes forward and makes NH₃.
Q < K means net forward, which makes NH₃. This mixes up the rule.
Q and K are compared with each other, not with 1. They differ by almost a factor of 2.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K, not from which gas has the higher pressure.

why.correct: Q is only meaningful next to the K of the same form: Q<sub>c</sub> with K<sub>c</sub> (molarities), Q<sub>p</sub> with K<sub>p</sub> (partial pressures in atm).
options: Right: Q and K can only be compared if they are built from the same kind of quantity.
With exponents that do not cancel (2 on top, 4 in total on the bottom), changing the quantity changes the value of Q.
The exponents are right, but moles are not pressures. The result cannot be compared with K<sub>p</sub>.
Concentrations belong in Q<sub>c</sub>, compared with K<sub>c</sub>. For K<sub>p</sub>, use partial pressures without brackets.

why.correct: Pure solids and pure liquids do not appear in K or Q, because their concentration is fixed by their density. Only gases and dissolved species are included.
options: Right: the two pure solids are left out, leaving only the gas.
Pure solids are left out of K: their "concentration" does not change however much solid is present.
This keeps the two solids and drops the gas, the opposite of the rule.
CO₂ is a product, so it goes on top.

why.correct: K<sub>c</sub> = [Zn²⁺] / [Cu²⁺]. Only Cu²⁺ is in the denominator; the solid metals are left out.
options: Right: a dissolved reactant, so it is in the denominator.
Zn²⁺ is a dissolved product, so it is in the numerator, not the denominator.
Zn is a reactant, but a pure solid is left out of K entirely.
A pure solid is left out of K.

why.correct: Write products over reactants and leave out pure liquids such as the solvent water.
options: Right: water is the liquid solvent, so it is left out.
Liquid water is the solvent; its concentration barely changes, so it is left out of K.
This is upside down. Products go in the numerator.
Concentrations in K are multiplied and divided, never added or subtracted.

why.correct: Q > K: the mixture holds too much product. The net reaction runs in reverse, which lowers Q, until Q = K.
options: Right: 25,000 > 4,000. The net reverse reaction lowers the product-to-reactant ratio until Q = K.
Making more product would raise Q further from K. The net reaction must go the other way.
Compare the powers of ten: 10⁴ is larger than 10³, so Q > K.
At equilibrium Q equals K. Here Q is more than six times K.

why.correct: Q has the same form as K but uses the current amounts. Comparing the two tells you which way the system must go to reach equilibrium.
Q and K have identical expressions. K is the value at equilibrium, which is fixed at a given temperature; Q is the value right now, which changes as the reaction runs.
options: Right: same expression, but K is the special value Q takes at equilibrium.
Both are products over reactants. Only the moment at which the amounts are measured differs.
Either can be written for gases (K<sub>p</sub>, Q<sub>p</sub> with pressures) or solutions (K<sub>c</sub>, Q<sub>c</sub>).
Solids and pure liquids are left out of both, so the two can be compared.

why.correct: At equilibrium Q = K: [NOCl]² / ([NO]²[Cl₂]) = 4.6 × 10⁴. So [NOCl]² = 4.6 × 10⁴ × (0.020)² × 0.010 = 0.184, and [NOCl] = √0.184 = 0.43 M.
At one temperature, every equilibrium mixture of the same reaction gives the same value of K, whatever amounts it started with. Small differences come from measurement precision.
options: Right: K comes out at about 50 every time (50.2, 49.9, 50.0), though the mixtures look nothing alike.
K is a ratio. Trial 3 has the most HI but also by far the most I₂, so the ratio [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) comes out about the same.
All three started differently, yet K is about the same. At a fixed temperature, K does not depend on the starting mixture.
[H₂] equals [I₂] only in trial 2. K is constant anyway.

why.correct: Use K from the trials (about 50.0). Q = 100 > K, so the net reverse reaction makes H₂ and I₂ until Q = K.
options: Right: Q = (0.0500)² / (0.0050 × 0.0050) = 100, twice K (about 50), so the net reaction goes in reverse.
Q > K means too much product, so HI must break down, not form.
K is fixed at a given temperature; the mixture changes to match K.
Direction comes from comparing Q with K. A large [HI] relative to [H₂] actually makes Q large.

why.correct: Concentrations first; then the ICE table links the one measured value to every other species through the coefficients; then substitute.
The solid is left out: K<sub>c</sub> = [NH₃][H₂S] = (0.0150)(0.0150) = 2.25 × 10⁻⁴.
Pure solids are left out of K and Q because their concentration is fixed. As long as some solid is present, the gas concentrations at equilibrium do not depend on how much solid there is.
options: Right: adding solid leaves Q = [NH₃][H₂S] unchanged, so Q still equals K and there is no shift.
The amount of a pure solid does not change its "concentration", so it does not change Q. Nothing shifts.
The reverse reaction is set by [NH₃][H₂S], which have not changed, so there is no net reaction.
Pressure and mass are not compared like this. The gas concentrations are fixed by K alone.

why.correct: A heterogeneous equilibrium involves species in more than one phase, such as a solid and gases. Its K leaves out the solid.
options: Right: a solid and gases, two phases.
All gases: one phase, a homogeneous equilibrium.
All gases: homogeneous.
All dissolved in one solution: homogeneous.

why.correct: K is defined for the equilibrium mixture. Starting concentrations give the value of Q at time zero; the system then changes until Q = K.
options: Right: only equilibrium values give the constant. Starting values give the reaction quotient at the start.
Precision is not the issue. Initial values describe a different state of the system.
K<sub>c</sub> is defined with molar concentrations, so molarity is correct.
Exponents come from coefficients and apply to equilibrium values. Squaring initial values does not fix the problem.

why.correct: Change row: A −x, B +2x. 2x = 0.20 M gives x = 0.10 M. Equilibrium [A] = 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 M.
options: Right: B rose by 2x = 0.20 M, so x = 0.10 M and A fell to 0.40 − 0.10 = 0.30 M.
This subtracts the change in B directly from A. A falls by x, which is half of B’s rise.
A reversible reaction does not use up its reactant; A remains at equilibrium.
A cannot stay at its starting value while B forms; B is made from A.

why.correct: The smaller K is, the less product the equilibrium mixture contains. K = 10⁻³¹ means the reaction barely proceeds.
options: Right: K = 4.5 × 10⁻³¹ is extremely small, so at equilibrium the product, NO, is present in a tiny amount.
K = 2.5 × 10³³ is huge: this reaction goes essentially to products.
K = 1.0 × 10⁵ is large, so products are favored.
K = 4.6 × 10⁻³ is small, so reactants are favored, but not nearly as strongly as in reaction 1.

why.correct: K describes the mixture once equilibrium is reached. How long that takes is kinetics (Unit 5). H₂ and Cl₂ can sit mixed in the dark for a long time, then react explosively in sunlight; K is the same either way.
options: Right: K is about the composition at equilibrium. Speed depends on the activation energy and the rate law, which K does not tell you.
K compares forward and reverse at equilibrium; a large K is compatible with both reactions being very slow.
Being product-favored says how much product there will be, not when. Some product-favored reactions take years.
K does not set the speed in either direction, so it cannot tell you the reaction is slow either.

why.correct: Compare exponents: the reaction with the largest K has the most product relative to reactant at equilibrium.
options: Right: it has the largest K, 2.5 × 10³³.
K = 1.0 × 10⁵ is large, but 10³³ is far larger.
K = 4.6 × 10⁻³ is below 1, so reaction 4 favors reactants.
Reaction 1 has the smallest K in the table; it favors reactants overwhelmingly.

why.correct: K much less than 1 means reactants are favored: some product forms, but most of the reactant is still there at equilibrium.
options: Right: K = 4.6 × 10⁻³. With [N₂O₄] near 1.0 M, [NO₂]² ≈ 4.6 × 10⁻³, so [NO₂] ≈ 0.068 M: a few percent reacts.
Starting with reactant only tells you the net reaction is forward (Q = 0 < K). It does not tell you how far it goes.
Every K is positive. What matters is whether K is much larger or much smaller than 1.
K < 1 does not mean zero product. Some NO₂ forms, just not much.

why.correct: The equilibrium mixture with the most product relative to reactant has the largest K. Count: I has 8 XY to 1 + 1 reactant molecules.
options: Right: K = 8² / (1 × 1) = 64, by far the most product per reactant.
K = 2² / (4 × 4) = 0.25, the smallest of the three.
K = 4² / (3 × 3) ≈ 1.8, in between.
Same starting amounts but different reactions settle at different mixtures, so the K values differ.

why.correct: A small K describes an equilibrium mixture that is mostly reactants. It is still an equilibrium: no further net change.
options: Right: K = 0.25, and the box holds 8 reactant molecules for every 2 product molecules.
Any equilibrium mixture contains some product. K > 1 needs products to outweigh reactants in the ratio, which they do not here.
The question says each container is at equilibrium. Mostly-reactant mixtures are common equilibria.
At equilibrium, Q = K and there is no net reaction, whatever the size of K.

why.correct: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, whatever the value of K. K describes the composition; the equal rates describe the dynamics.
options: Right: equal rates define equilibrium for every reaction; K > 1 or K < 1 only describes where the amounts end up.
K > 1 means more product at equilibrium, not a larger forward rate at equilibrium. At equilibrium the rates are equal.
If the reverse rate were larger, the composition would still be changing. It is at equilibrium.
Constant composition comes from equal rates, not zero rates.
